utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar, good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. The Chamber would like to put a few questions to the next witness in closed session before giving a decision on the protective measures sought, so we will first turn into private session -- closed session and then I will ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, may I ask you to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. DP30, because that's how we will call you from now on since a decision has been taken granting protective measures in respect of you. Before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. DP30. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by counsel for the Defence. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. DP30, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I start asking you question I am going to show you a document and you can confirm to us whether the information that has been included on this sheet of paper is correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: The information is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, although we have heard a lot of information about Mr. DP30, perhaps we could just go very briefly into closed session in order to get certain other information about his background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will turn into private session. Ms. Pilipovic what we heard before was information in respect of a decision on protective measures and not part of the evidence. It has not been given under a solemn declaration. So I think it would be necessary to repeat such issues if -- for evidentiary reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, you told us that your family left Sarajevo. Can you tell us whether there were any particular reasons for which your family was treated in the way it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, I have already said that they knew -- everyone knew that I worked in Pale. So that the propaganda conducted towards the JNA members - and my Muslim colleagues were astounded by it - this was directed to me, too. I was called to the barracks, I was called up and they said, "you've got nothing to do here, you are part of the Serbian and Chetnik Army."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, thank you. I want to tell you that we will be talking about the period September 1992 - August 1994. Were you militarily engaged during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes, I was militarily engaged during that period. I was commander of the warehouse of ammunition and materiel and equipment in Koran and at Pale. It was within the 27th Logistics Base of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, you say you were the commander of the warehouse of ammunition weapons at Koran. Can you tell us when the 27th Logistics Base was formed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was formed immediately following departure of the JNA from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina because that was a short period during which the JNA withdrew with its equipment and its units, and the few of us who remained there were -- in fact, I had no where else to go anymore because I couldn't go to Croatia, so I stayed where I had work and assumed the duties that all those who were fit for military service had. And the command at the beginning, it remained blocked in the Marshal Tito Barracks in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP30, when you say that your command was captured in the Marshal Tito Barracks, can you tell us whether you went to your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did. I went to the command, to meetings, that was usually once a week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you went for the meeting for the last time in the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, the last time I was at a meeting in the command was toward the end of March, and after that I didn't go again. We only had a telephone line which we had, as far as I can remember, until the end of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that your command remained in the barracks and that for a short period of time it was captured, can you tell us when your command, that is to say the people who worked in the command, when did they leave the command, do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the command left in the first half of June, around the first half of June, together with the cadets and the officers who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, when you say that your command was there and you've just mentioned cadets, too, cadets from the school centre of the JNA, do you personally know whether there was any ammunition in the Marshal Tito Barracks, whether there were any weapons there and do you know what happened to those weapons after the members of the school centre and of your command left the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, there was an infantry school centre there for training NCOs and officers from the infantry, that was for the entire JNA. And as far as I can remember there was a school for quartermaster officers and noncommissioned officers. And as in all training centres, there were all sorts of weapons, especially infantry weapons, and then there were some tanks there. I think they were T-55 tanks, because I passed by them. There were three or five of them. I can't give you the exact number. Then there were armoured personnel carriers for the infantry, OTM-60 and combat vehicles for the infantry, BB-5 M-80, that was the mark, and then there were four-wheel drives, freight vehicles, that's what was parked by the garages, the playground and the workshop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know personally know, after the withdrawal of the command and the schools, what happened to those weapons, were they withdrawn too or do you know anything else about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Since these men left or they passed through Pale, and the captured command, the members of the command passed through my barracks, so they weren't able to take anything apart from their personal weapons and equipment with them. Everything else remained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP30, when you say that from September 1992 to August 1994, that's the period that we are dealing with you said that you were the commander of ammunition of the 27th Logistics Base, can you tell us out of which warehouses was the 27th Logistics Base formed? According to your knowledge, what entered into the 27th Logistics Base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well the 27th Logistics Base consisted of those warehouses which remained in Serbian territory, or rather it was the way that the people had divided up from the first barricades in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo. So my warehouse remained there. And then as far as I can remember, the Rudo and Visegrad warehouses, the Vardiste warehouse, Ilijas, Semizovac, Butile and Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, you said that division was made as far as I have understood you when the barricades were set up in Sarajevo, and the surrounding area, can you tell us whether you know whether they were warehouses which were not on the Serbian side, as you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes. Those -- there were the warehouses which on the basis of that division -- because of that division remained on the other side. That was the warehouse in Visoko. I don't know how much equipment remained there. Then there was Krupanjska Rijeka near Hadzici, Ljuta near Konjic and Usti Kolina in the vicinity of Gorazde. And I apologise, there was also the Renovica warehouse from August 1992 when the Muslim forces took that warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague suggests that something is missing in the transcript. The exact words that the witness said with regard to certain places are missing in the transcript. I think he said Ljuta near Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, could you please repeat the names of the warehouses you have mentioned and that you said remained on the Muslim side. Could you say the names slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: The Visoko warehouse, then Krupanjska Rijeka warehouse between Hadzici and Pazarici, Ljuta near Konjic, Usti Kolina, that is close to Gorazde, and Renovica from the end of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, you said Renovica from August 1992. Can you tell us what area the Renovica warehouse was located in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: The Renovica warehouse was about 30 kilometres from Pale in the direction of Gorazde. At the beginning of the war, the Serbian forces held it and it was also my warehouse branch, it was under my command. However, since there were constant threats, there was constant danger, the Muslim forces kept attacking and the soldiers and reserves could have been captured, so we took out some of the reserve and the Muslim forces attacked, and that part was surrendered by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP30. When you said -- when you mentioned these warehouses, you mentioned warehouses of the former JNA in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the warehouses of the JNA which were part of the 744 Logistics Base which was the base of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP30, do you personally know whether in the area of the town of Sarajevo, do you know whether there were any similar warehouses there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence had warehouses too. Part of the warehouses of the Territorial Defence were in barracks, and there was a big warehouse, the Faletici warehouse which is in the north-eastern part of Sarajevo, immediately next to the periphery, that was a warehouse of the Territorial Defence, that is to say, of the town headquarters of Sarajevo. I know about that because when I was serving in Zenica, I had reserve battalion in that warehouse for nuclear, biological and chemical defence. So I often entered that warehouse, I often went into it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, you say that you often went into that warehouse. Can you tell us whether you saw any weapons in that warehouse and if so of what kind, if you saw any weapons there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, the Territorial Defence mostly formed light infantry brigades, so the weapons and the equipment were the weapons and equipment for a light infantry brigade on the whole. On the whole, this was infantry weapons, mortars, rifles, automatic weapons, 60, 82-millimetre and 120-millimetre mortars. Part of the weapons for anti-aircraft defence were included there. There were 12.7 millimetre machine-guns, field guns, 20 through 1 and 20 through 3 there were anti-armour guided missiles, 9-K11 recoilless field guns, 82-millimetres [Realtime transcript read in error "82-millimetre metres"], communication equipment, part of the vehicles, and on the whole that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, you've just mentioned the various kinds of weapons that were based in the Faletici warehouse and that was part of the Territorial Defence of the town of Sarajevo. Can you tell us how these weapons were stored? Did you see this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, the weapons in accordance with the rules of the JNA which were applied by the Territorial Defence, all the weapons that were stored there had visible Territorial Defence markings, a four-figure number, and then it said whether it was platoon, a company, a detachment. Everything had been marked, each piece of equipment, and similarly lorries, there were stickers on the window with the Territorial Defence sign, and it said how long the equipment would be valid. Every piece of equipment was marked in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the sake of the transcript, line 5 of the current page, perhaps we could say what weapon is concerned against because "82-millimetre metre" doesn't mean much to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, when you told about the weapons in the Faletici warehouse, you spoke about 9K-11 recoilless field guns and then you mentioned 82-millimetre what? Because in English it appears not to be clear. Could you please repeat that answer in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. When I mentioned mortars, I mentioned 60-millimetre mortars, 82-millimetre mortars and 120-millimetre mortars. And then when I mentioned a recoilless 82-millimetre field gun and the anti-armoured guided missiles, so-called Maljutkas, 9 through 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, does this sufficiently clarify the issue? Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, did you personally know, we are talking about the year 1992, did you know under whose control the Territorial Defence warehouse in Faletici was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: In 1992, the Faletici warehouse was under the JNA, or rather the JNA held guard there, stood guard there. I don't know how many soldiers there were as part of the guard, but I don't think there were many. These were mostly soldiers from the Lukavica Barracks, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether throughout the period of 1992 they guarded that warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: No, that was towards the beginning of May or the end of April and the Territorial Defence or rather the people led by the Territorial Defence entered that warehouse. The Muslims forces entered on one side and the Serbian on the other and those weapons were taken out and all the equipment, even the vehicles, everything that was there, I think that the Serbian side got most of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP30, you said that you were the chief, the commander of the warehouse and ammunition in Koran, can you tell us, in the 27th Logistics Base, did any staff remain there? Did any personnel remain there who worked before the conflict broke out in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: In my warehouse mostly soldiers who were doing their military service in Bosnia-Herzegovina remained. Those were mostly Serbian men, Serbian soldiers. Some of them were Muslims who, in spite of Alija Izetbegovic's appeal not to respond to the JNA call-up, neither as active or reserve forces, certain individuals did respond, individuals who were in favour of Yugoslavia, and there was some Croats, but a smaller number. So the warehouse was mostly staffed by Serbs. Over 90 per cent were Serbs and all the others were of other nationality. That was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that that was at the beginning, could you be a little more precise and tell us which period you are referring to, the period during which there were Serbs and Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, that was up until about the beginning of July. I know that I had another three Muslim soldiers who were doing their military service and I then sent them to Belgrade in a bus. I know that I suggested that they shouldn't return to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later, a sergeant contacted me from the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you telling us that in your 27th Logistics Base as far as the men are concerned, Serbs and Croats remained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Mostly Serbs and a few Croats who were there and who lived in the territory of the municipality of Pale because that is in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, in 1992, September, during the period of September 1992, August 1994, can you tell us whether your warehouse provided units of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps with ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us were you under the direct command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: No. I was not under the direct command. It was through my command I was the commander of the logistics base and their base was in Sokolac. I was under the command of the Main Staff, that is, my base was under the command of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you told us that you supplied the SRK units with ammunition, can you tell us what was the procedure of supplying ammunition to the SRK units? Was there a person representing the SRK that you contacted, with whom you communicated or was there another way that you supplied the ammunition to the units of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, the procedure is well known which -- and it is regulated by the rules before as in the JNA and then the Army of Republika Srpska took it over -- according to the rules of supply and maintenance of technical equipment. So the request of the corps go to the corps, the technical department gathers them, and then send them directly to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, I apologise. You will continue. Can you just explain, I think you said that on the level of the SRK there was also a technical department. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. There were chiefs of services with their assistants and they looked after the logistics support to the corps units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was the chief of the technical section for the Sarajevo Romanija Corps when you were the commander of the warehouse of the 27th Logistics Base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Where I was the commander of the warehouse of the 27th Logistics Base, I know that this was Milivoje Solar who was the chief. He was lieutenant-colonel of the technical corps, the technical apartment. He was the chief of the technical department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP30, can you tell us about the request of the corps seeking ammunition, requesting ammunition who were they supplied to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: The request of the corps asking requesting for ammunition were to the main corps of the Republika Srpska Army and then the main staff would approve the requested quantities of ammunition depending on the possibilities and then by return, they would respond by contacting the command of the logistics base, and the basis of that, the chief of the technical service would then give Scheduling Order which I would then receive at the warehouse and that's how I issued ammunition to the brigades, depending on the Scheduling Order, that's how I would issue ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30 can you tell us whether there were situations when following the reception of the Scheduling Order for the ammunition for the brigades, did you have personal authorisation to change this request?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: No, I was not able to do it, nor was I authorised to do this because the reports about the supplying of ammunition we then had to pass on to the commander of logistics base and then to the Main Staff, and they were the one who were looking after the ammunition quantities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the request for ammunition, a certain amount of ammunition would be approved that you were authorised to issue to the brigades. Can you tell us who would then take over this ammunition that was approved, according to the request?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Since my warehouse had only about 30 per cent of manpower levels filled and that's how much the transport vehicles were also filled up, the units came to take ammunition themselves. That was how it worked. And sometimes we would use our own transport vehicles to take the ammunition, but mostly that didn't happen so often. So there was also this combined system of supply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that sometimes you used your own transport vehicles to supply the ammunition, can you tell us the reason why is it that you were able to sometimes do it? Was this something that you did as a matter of course or were there other reasons that you wouldn't be able to transport the ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: I already said that I didn't have many vehicles, many means of transport in relation to the formation levels, the manpower levels, that was one reason. The second reason was that the main duty of my warehouse was to take out the ammunition produced at the Pretis factory, and my duty was to first take this ammunition to my warehouse, and then report to the Main Staff through my base command in order to supply and distribute this ammunition to other bases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, when you told us that the ammunition was produced at the Pretis factory and that you had the obligation to, as you say, take out this ammunition can you tell us what kind of ammunition was produced at Pretis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Mostly as I remember, first of all, this was the ammunition for mortars, that is shells of 60, 82, and 120-millimetre calibres. There was artillery ammunition for Howitzers, 105 millimeters, 122 millimeters, and there were two kinds, D-30, and there was another M-38 type. Then for Howitzer, 155 millimetre, then there was possibly ammunition for antitank field guns, 106 millimetre, 110 millimetres, T-12, 100 millimetre tanks, then grenades for multiple rocket launchers, or rockets for multiple rocket launchers, and I think for recoilless guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, you have just listed the type of ammunition, the types of ammunition that was produced, and you say that this was the production at Pretis factory. Can you tell us whether this ammunition in this way that you have identified it, was this marked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes. The ammunition has to be marked both in peace and at war, and it is very important so that there is no switch that can be made. So that instead of, say, signaling equipment, signaling mines or smoke grenades, then combat ammunition is issued. So the same way as it was marked in JNA, that's how it was marked here, that is with in Cyrillic characters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you are telling us about the ammunition production, you are telling us about the period 1992, 1994, can you tell us what was the capacity, how much of this ammunition was produced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, it was very much reduced and this depended on several factors. First of all, in this factory only Serbs remained to work in this factory. And before the war, this ammunition was produced for the supplies to the entire JNA, and also went abroad, particularly to the nonaligned companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, when you are telling us about the ammunition that was produced at the time at the Pretis factory, and which arrived to your 27th Logistics Base, can you tell us whether all of this ammunition was to be used by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: I think I may have already spoken about this. The ammunition that was produced there and the main obligation was for it to come to my warehouse, then depending on the Scheduling Order of the Main Staff, it was distributed to the other three bases, that is, the base that was in Banja Luka. I think they were the 14th Logistics Base. Then there was the base in Bijeljina, I think that was the 35th Logistics Base, and then the base in Bileca. I think that was the 30th Logistics Base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, are you tell us that this production was meant for the entire Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes, that's where it was produced, the ammunition, as I listed it, for the entire army for Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, can you tell us, according to military rules, your base, was it supposed to fall under the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes, according to army rules, every corps has to have its own logistics base from which they have supply for their units, but in this case this was not so, according to the ruling or the decision of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that your base supplied also other corps or units in the territory of the Republika Srpska Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: I already said about the artillery ammunition, that it went to all the other bases, what was produced in Pretis, but as far as my base is concerned, I believe that it was from November 1992 that the newly formed Drina Corps [Realtime transcript read in error "unit corps"] also depended on my base. So I think that was also one of the reasons why the Main Staff decided that this base would be directly under their command, under its command, the command of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, can you tell us whether your warehouse was only warehouse for ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: My warehouse wasn't just ammunition warehouse because it was slightly further away from the first front lines. There were other means that were also there, that is quartermasters' equipment, that is for kitchens and so on. Everything else that an army needs. There were also means, other kinds of equipment, engines, then also some veterinary equipment, and some medical supplies, a smaller part of medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague is saying that the transcript -- in the transcript there is not been entered properly, I believe that is on page 25, line 5, that not the correct formulation for a Drina corps had been entered in the transcript

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes it is my recollection that the newly established Drina corps was also served by the logistics base. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, now that you have listed for us what military equipment and other reserves of materiel were kept in your warehouse, can you tell us considering that you worked there all the time and you were the person who was in charge of issuing ammunition, can you tell us about the ammunition, the use of ammunition from your warehouse or possibly, can you tell us about ammunition that was stored in your warehouse, first of all, so that you can then answer about the use of which ammunition. So, first of all, can you tell us what type of ammunition did you have in your warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: I will try, if I can remember everything. Mostly in my warehouse there were all kinds of infantry ammunition, that is from pistols, 7.62, 7.55. Then for rifles, light machine-guns, automatic rifles, 7.62 millimeters, domestic production, 7.9 millimeters. Then there was ammunition for AA -- anti-aircraft machine-guns, Browning guns, 12.7, and then 14.5 millimeters. Then for Praga, 30 millimeters. Then the ammunition that I have already mentioned, that is, artillery ammunition manufactured at Pretis. Then also antitank guided rockets, 9K-11. Then there was Strela 2M anti-aircraft. Then for recoilless guns, 82-millimetre. Then ammunition for tanks. Mostly I already mentioned the anti-infantry -- the anti-personnel, anti-aircraft and for artillery support, that's the ammunition that was kept there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP30, can you tell us what was the use of this ammunition, and we are speaking about the period between 1992 through to 1994? Can you personally answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes. According to my estimate, in the first six months I cannot say that this has all been used, it's all been issued, I was the one who was issuing. I don't know what the use was. But for the first six months, there were -- there was more issuing compared the period following that one, while I was the commander of the warehouse and I was the commander until January of 1994. So after that first period it was reduced, significantly reduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that in the first six months there was more issuing of ammunition, more ammunition was issued, can you tell us whether you personally have the knowledge why in this first six months, in which period is that in 1992, which six months in 1992 are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: In that period in the first six months that's when mostly the brigades were formed as part of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. So the issue influenced directly the establishment of the reserves of these brigades which were supposed to be established, according to the military rules. And mostly for that reason that the issuing was increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told us that the issuing was in connection with the establishment of brigades which became part of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Do you personally know, considering your answer, what personnel were members of these brigades, and do you know which brigades are they in those first six months, as you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, before the witness answers this question, one of the previous questions put to you has not been answered yet. The six month, which six month are you talking about? The first six months starting when, exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, thank you, Your Honour. Yes, in relation to 1992, yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. DP30, can you tell us, in your opinion this period of six months when does it start this period that is linked to the establishment of brigades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: That period starting from the beginning of May, that's where the VRS was established, until October. That's the period. Because from the 1st of November, that's when Drina Corps also started to be supplied, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are now telling us about the establishment of brigades during this period from the moment when the Army of Republika Srpska was established. Can you tell us do you have any knowledge which brigades are they and who entered into the composition of the brigades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: These were mostly seven brigades that were part of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. That is they were established mostly the members were Serbs, Serb whose were leaving Sarajevo, whether also Serbs were leaving Central Bosnia, leaving municipalities of Zenica, Busovaca, Kakanj some of them left Visoko, possibly Kiseljak, all of these people leaving left via the area of Sarajevo where there was the Serb cross-roads, so to speak. And most of these Serbs joined these brigades and that's how the manpower personnel was filled. Ilidza, Ilijas, the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade. I think it was 1st Rajlovac and then Vogosca Brigade. Then there was the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade and also there was the 1st Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP30, when we are speaking about your warehouse and the ammunition that was stored there in the area of the Koran warehouse, can you tell us in which way was maintenance done, the maintenance of the ammunition? What were the maintenance conditions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: As far as ammunition is concerned there was no particular maintenance that had to be kept except the usual measures, according to regulations, for storing of ammunition. Because if was stored mostly in stable facilities. And as far as the other technical equipment and materiel my base had as part of the barracks where I was, there was a company of maintenance support and that is the medium maintenance support, that is of medium degree of maintenance support, and from the brigades some equipment that wasn't working would come to be fixed, for instance, vehicles, communication equipment. And sometimes for artillery weapons and for heavier armoured vehicles, then teams were sent to the locations where these means were, where the equipment was and that's where the maintenance or the repair was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, are you telling us that as part of your house there was also a section for repairing the weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in your opinion the way of storing ammunition can influence the good working order of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, the weapons is outside during at wartime. All weapons are outside which means that they are exposed to weather conditions, all weather conditions. That means the cold, snow, rain, mud. And in the middle of combat it is not always possible to maintain the weapons in field conditions as it is done in peace. So it is logical that in these conditions there were more breakdowns, that the weapons is then used up more quickly, so to speak. There is also the corrosion process which damages particularly the barrels of weapons. And then -- then it could be that weapons could then have to have larger calibre and then of course they would also be imprecise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to inform you that my colleague will continue with the examination for the time that remains for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If my computer starts functioning, I would like to ask you a few questions about technical matters. Do you know what one usually calls maintenance? Do you know what that is? Not exactly. For the English booth the term "remontage" is not maintenance. Just use the term "remontage". Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: "Remontage" or maintenance includes basic maintenance by immediate user, by the direct users. It involve certain measures that the operators have to carry out on a daily basis. Furthermore, there is a sort of light maintenance which is done in workshops in the brigade --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will interrupt you there. When I say "remontage," I am talking about mortars, specifically. What sort of operations of remontage are carried out with mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Ammunition is also subjected to remontage after a certain period of time. It is -- there is then a sort of interim and general remontage of ammunition. Part of the ammunition is taken to test whether it still as the characteristics that are required of it. If it is not satisfactory the ammunition is subjected to remontage or it is disposed of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked about an ammunitions factory with which you worked at the period of the events. This ammunitions factory, did it also get involved in remontage in relation to mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: The ammunition factory wasn't with us and remontage of the ammunition was carried out by the technical workshop as part of the 14th logistics base in Banja Luka. And it was capable of doing this in peacetime, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, does the age of ammunition -- is the age of ammunition a factor which leads to such or requires such remontage; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, clearly the age is a factor. If we talk about a powder charge, it has a certain age. It grows old in chemical terms and no longer satisfies conditions or rather when the powder burns, the effects that are required of certain types of ammunition are not obtained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know whether the stocks of ammunition, supplies of ammunition that the parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina had at their disposal, do you know whether at the time of the hostilities, do you know whether these ammunition supplies were fairly old; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, mostly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So far, Mr. President, we don't have a proper basis for this witness to be asked that question in terms of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, although the question has been answered, I would like to ask about his knowledge which seems evident to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Witness, in relation to a question that I am going to ask you about the age of the ammunition, do you know or did you know, did you have at the time any information about this matter, that is to say, about the age of the ammunition, and if you had any information about this, where did you obtain this information from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, that information was on the cases of ammunition. You could quite clearly see when it was assembled and the year of assembly. You could see ammunition and it bore these markings, this information. It was applicable for all ammunition apart from the latest automatic weapons, the 6.7-millimetre rifle ammunition was fairly new and it hadn't been the subject of remontage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now ask you about artillery and mortars, for example which were used by the artillery or by the infantry at the beginning of the conflict. How old was the ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I gather from Mr. Piletta-Zanin's response at page 32, line 14, that he intends to rely upon the part answer given by the witness to the question to which I objected. The response by the witness to the further question establishes only a basis of knowledge for ammunition which was provided to the Bosnian Serb forces, not the other forces, therefore, I seek that witness's answer be redacted on page 32, at approximately line 10. Alternatively, that it be clearly understood that it relates only to Bosnian Serb ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think that there is any redaction here because we are talking about cases of ammunition, and we know that these cases were the same on both sides of the line. We have always been aware of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, whether that is true or not is a second issue. Please try to get precise answers on the issue you would like to deal with. That means that you are talking about the beginning of the outbreak of the conflict. Perhaps ask with some precision what ammunition you specifically would like to have information about because from the answers it is clear that your questions leave open so much that it is really guessing on what the witness will testify about, rather than to guide him with -- without leading him, but guiding him with sufficient precision to get answers that could assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- The Prosecution is deeply concerned that Mr. Piletta-Zanin made the comment in the presence of the witness and in my respectful submission the only remedy to overcome that prejudice is for the Defence to be disallowed from asking any more questions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided to put a few questions to the witness in respect of the subject just dealt with. When you are talking about ammunition, when you are talking about boxes of ammunition, what boxes are you talking about? Boxes you've seen where and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I talk about the ammunition that was stocked in my warehouse in accordance with the regulations, every type of ammunition has its own kind of packaging. The rules are very specific. The length, the width, the height, and it bears the number of the packaging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question: What do you know about boxes of ammunition used by the other party in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about the ammunition that the other side used in the conflict, but I can assume that reserve ammunition that was in the Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you take it that ammunition from the Territorial Defence might have been used by the other party; is that how I understand your answer? But do you have any personal knowledge of the ammunition used by the other party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed and on the basis of the answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as remontage, maintenance and overhaul is concerned, and since there were inscriptions on the cases, could you tell this Chamber whether the ammunition that wasn't at the disposition of your army at the beginning of your hostilities, can you confirm that this ammunition was already fairly old, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question because it is in a leading form and any further questioning by the counsel should not be leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will put that question differently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what can you say with regard to the age of the ammunition that was used? And I am referring to the mortars at the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: I already said that there was ammunition which included grenades which were fairly old and which had even been re-assembled. These were stocks of the federal reserve for the JNA. Among those reserve stocks, there were stocks that had been produced quite a long time ago that were fairly old. At the time there was no war and it was normal for ammunition to be stocked and kept until it was to be used, and until it was disposed of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us any information about the age of the ammunition and any general information about the average age; yes or no? If you can't, well, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: There was 7.9 millimetre ammunition which had been produced in 1947 and 1952. I remember that very well from the cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: I couldn't give you any precise information about mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know what firing tables are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes, firing tables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, with regard to the problem concerning remontage, maintenance and overhaul, what could you tell us about firing tables, that is to say would these firing tables have to be brought up to date, et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes. After maintenance and overhaul, if the ammunition doesn't satisfy all the conditions in accordance with the previous tables, new ones are issued according to which you take certain measures when targeting, and you follow these steps when firing in order to ensure that the ammunition is precise, given the conditions that prevail at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, as a result, and this is a purely theoretical question, if I wanted to determine the trajectory of a mortar shell with regard to -- in relation to a shell that had been re-assembled, I should base myself on the adapted firing table for this re-assembled mortar. Is that how I am to understand your testimony; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness we will now move on to another subject. Could you tell us what tracer bullets are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, tracer bullets are bullets which usually there is a tracer at the back with a security compound, and at night you can usually see the trajectory of the bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a difference between a tracer bullet and an incendiary bullet; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know whether in the ex-JNA, in the former JNA, and in times of war, do you know whether there was a manner of using ammunition, that is to say, to put ammunition in weapons themselves, to divide tracer ammunition and nontracer ammunition amongst the weapons themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, usually in combat kits and packets, yes, the ammunition was distributed in this way. This concerned infantry ammunition in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But when one is loading one's weapon, if you know anything about this, were there any orders that had been given to the men concerning loading their weapons, that is to say whether tracer bullets should be used or nontracer bullets or a mixture of the two, should there be a certain distribution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, for some information -- for some ammunition, for some machine-guns, the ammunition had been sorted in this way. I couldn't say whether every 3rd or 5th bullet was a tracer one. But with regard to infantry weapons, yes, there are mixed packages too, PZO indications. It means "tracer" ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can these tracer bullets also be seen during the day? You talked about the night, but in daytime, under certain conditions, is it possible to see the trace of the so-called tracer bullets; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes, such tracer bullets can be seen even in the daytime when visibility is not that good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would now like to move on to the subject of craters. During the events were you able to see any craters in the area that you were familiar with, that is to say, where you worked during the war; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: I saw some craters in Pale when the first half of July, August, when Pale was shelled. I think it was caused by the -- they were caused by Howitzer shells and in the vicinity of the Military Hospital I saw them and in the vicinity of my barracks, a few shells fell there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of crater -- what types of crater did you see, what weapon was used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion these were weapons that had a fairly long range. I think Howitzers or field guns were used because we didn't find any that hadn't exploded so it wasn't possible to say what caused the craters exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the origin of fire was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Well, as the artillery men from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps assessed it, it came from the direction of Sarajevo, from that direction on the whole. So it seemed that only the elevation of the barrel was being moved, altered, because the direction of fire was always the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, did you have the opportunity of seeing any other craters, apart from craters caused by field guns or Howitzers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes. Especially after the war in 1997 and 1998 when I got involved in the mine clearance process, and when I worked with mine clearers in minefields and which were, on the whole, between the demarcation lines of the two sides. Near the lines of the sides in the conflict, there were craters, and often we would find mortar shells there that had not exploded. Usually if a mortar shell hasn't exploded, we would often find the safety valve in it so that meant the person that fired the mortar shell did not take the safety valve out so the shell did not explode. And if an explosion occurred, there was the corresponding crater and its size depended on the calibre and the crater also depended on what the ground was composed of, whether it was a sandy ground or whether the ground was hard or whether it was an asphalt or concrete surface, that's the case when the crater is not very deep and then you can see the traces of the explosion and the traces of the shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will stop you there. Witness, did you have the opportunity of seeing craters and craters caused by mortar shells during the wartime period too, because your answer concerned the period after the war. But from 1992 to 1994, during that period, did you have the opportunity of seeing such craters; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would now like to return to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, perhaps, Mr. President, Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 17002 to 17011. we should go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment. We now are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as a superior officer or senior officer, have you ever seen any order that would have been of racist nature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Considering that you've answered now, have you ever, as a senior officer, seen or heard about a plan, at the level of the corps of the army, which was racist in nature; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, have you ever heard it said, more precisely, that the Army Corps would have issued a plan destined to eradicate all Muslim population from Sarajevo; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said earlier that you didn't know about the weapons cases of the opposing side. But what do you know about the locations from which the opposing side was getting its weapons in an initial period, either time when the conflict broke out, when the war started and then during the later period, during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: What can I tell you, what I've already said, that it was from the warehouse of Faletici that the opposing side also got weapons and the military equipment. And everything else I can just presume or suppose because there were other channels that were used and that was disclosed on television, and even under the auspices of international forces that weapons were produced in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will stop you now. You are speaking about the Faletici warehouse. Do you know what could have been in Faletici? Were there also ammunitions and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question. Madam Pilipovic questioned the witness at length about the weaponry that was in the warehouse at Faletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know. I know. But what I wanted to clarify by this, Mr. President, was the type of cases, of boxes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is my recollection that the witness answered a question that he assumed that the opposite party would have taken it, but it was not his knowledge. So the only remaining question that would be whether the witness knew anything about the cases in the Faletici warehouse. Do you know anything about the cases in the Faletici warehouse? Did you ever see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please tell us what you know about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you what I saw. I said that I went there and that I had a unit which was part of the war reserves. And it is normal when we went there for control that the people who were handling, who had issued, been issued with these weapons, they socialised, they would air the premises and occasionally a unit from the technical section would be working and they are on the reconservation of weapons and of other equipment. And of course that's where I saw, apart from the equipment, I also saw the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What could you tell us about the ammunition? What type of ammunition was it, for what weaponry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly for the weapons that were there, that were stored there for that unit. So that would be anti-personnel, and then shells for mortars, 60, 82, and 120-millimetre calibre. Then there was ammunition for AA machine-guns, for AA guns, 20 through 3, 20 through 11, 20 through 1, 20 to 3 millimetre, and also for recoilless guns, and then for anti-tank rockets of the Zolja and Osa types, and also guided rockets for 9K-11 weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the boxes in which the ammunition was stored? Could you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are boxes, cases with standard issue and standard packaging. The size is the same as the JNA had. This was former -- done by former factories of the former SFRJ and the factories that produced the ammunition for the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on these boxes that we are speaking about, was there a year that was written on those boxes, the year of fabrication, the year of production?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes, within the code. The year of production would be included in the code.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we are speaking about mortar shells, do you recall what were these numbers on the boxes that we were able to see, to which years were these numbers referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness or to start to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the answer is yes to both questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You will now be examined by counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. DP30. Cross-examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during your training and indeed your education before your training, were you ever taught English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any understanding of the English language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: A little bit, what I've learned in the process of humanitarian mine clearance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were interviewed by an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor for the Tribunal on the 8th of July 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think present also was Richard Philipps and Michael Blaxill, and they also asked you some questions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you questioned with the assistance of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you responded to their questions, did you do so truthfully and to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the questions asked by those three gentlemen interpreted into a language that you could understand, and if so, what language was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30
utterances.text: The interpreter interpreted into the language I could understand, which is Bosnian or Croatian or Serbian, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to make a submission in private session in the absence of the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I would like to turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 12.51 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will turn into open session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we are in open session again. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness, which would be Witness DP2? Yes. Madam Usher, could you then please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please check on whether channel 6 is on. Can you now hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. DP2 because that's how we will call you, Mr. DP2, since protective measures have been granted in respect of you. That means that no one outside this courtroom will see your face and we will not use your name. Mr. DP2, before giving evidence in this court, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration and the text will be handed out to you now by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with pleasure. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. DP2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: Good morning or good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we start anything, we are going to show you a document which is already in the hands of Madam Usher, I believe. And as soon as you have a look at the information contained in the document, let us know if the information given is correct; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: Yes, they are correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would like to ask questions of personal nature. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you ever served under arms during the period of the conflict in Sarajevo? If you can answer with a yes or no, I would be grateful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not? Why didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: I didn't bear weapons because I did not wish to do that, but I was mobilised into the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, what did you do during the war since apparently you were not defending the country and bearing arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: During the war I had two duties, one was the work obligation at the republican pedagogical institute where I worked as an expert advisor, and the second work obligation was a war one. I was digging trenches and I think I am a rare example of a citizen of Sarajevo which had two work obligations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Every time you used in Serbian -- as you used in Serbian the word "obligation" when you were speaking about the work obligation in relation to digging of trenches, Witness, was this something that was voluntarily or not? Because one can take on an obligation voluntarily, and the opposite is equally true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: No, that was not a voluntarily obligation. Initially, I dug trenches because I was rounded up in the street. And later on I regularly received call-up papers to go and dig trenches from the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know -- no, I withdraw that. Have you ever refused this obligation, this work obligation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't even think of that. And I think I wouldn't dare refuse such an obligation because to be a Serb in Sarajevo, not to take up a weapon and to refuse to dig would mean a kind of suicide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more precise, please? Could you be more precise, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: Well, precise answer would be that Serbs in Sarajevo lost their lives just because they would have a Serb name. And to refuse to dig trenches would mean a provocation in a sense that people would come to my apartment, take me away and I would disappear. That would be something that would irritate them, that would give them a cause to make something happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you say that you would disappear, what did you mean by that, specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: Well, it's not unknown that Serbs disappeared in Sarajevo. People would enter at night into their apartments. Whoever had a weapon, had a rifle, had some kind of accreditation and could enter into an apartment and take away the person. To disappear in Sarajevo, that would mean to be neither dead or alive, but more frequently, dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that this was something that was well known. Do you personally have knowledge of such facts, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do. That was well known in Sarajevo that Serbs disappeared, that they were murdered. Some of my friends also disappeared like that. And I have to say that every night as soon as darkness fell I would expect and would be anxious when my turn would come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you say that some of your friends have disappeared in this abrupt way. I would like you to tell us more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. President, I believe we are going to be to go back into closed session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can tell us some names, but as soon as we are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, again we are in open session now. You spoke of this Mr. Caco earlier. Is there an event in particular in relation to the elimination of people, no matter who they were, that you can tell us about and to which you were present at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: It is known that Caco Topolovic had problems in the town also with the official police. And until the final event, the 27th of October, 1993, when finally the police had the final showdown with Caco, during that showdown of Muslims, I was a hostage with my wife and with 60 of our neighbours. I was present when Caco killed 8 policemen with his handgun in their mouths and in front of 60 of us hostages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, Caco lost his life and the trial showed that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I apologise. The interpreters are asking you to repeat the very last sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you can say from the moment when you were speaking about 60 hostages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: In front of 60 hostages that Caco held under the threat that unless Alija Izetbegovic with his police and army, if Alija Izetbegovic attacks him, that he will then kill us. Then in front of us, I said he cut the throats of two policemen. And before that, he killed 8 hostages with a gun in their mouth, with a pistol in their mouth, and I watched that and I was not the only one who saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. In relation to this person that you spoke about, this man called Caco, do you know what was his military significance; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are still missing one part of an answer in the transcript. You told us that Caco died and that something became apparent at the trial, but there was not -- is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I didn't say that the transcript was not reflecting what the witness said. What I said was that we may have had a problem of redaction in relation to the information disclosed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked Madam Registrar to deal with that. And I came to my next point, that was that you told us something about Caco that died and that something became apparent at trial. But that part of your answer is not clearly reflected in the transcript. So would you please repeat what you said about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Caco didn't die, he was killed. On that day when police and army were sent on him, against him, after that members of his staff were arrested and some soldiers. I know that there was a trial and at this trial crimes were spoken of during this trial, the crimes that Caco had committed against the Serb population in Sarajevo. If I may, the investigator at this trial neuropsychiatrist, Dragan Stanic, who is an acquaintance of mine, told me that those 30 of Caco's combatants admitted to having killed over 700 Serb civilians at Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object on the basis of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked the witness to tell this. But I think he -- you finished your answer in this respect -- on this subject. I have got one more question: When was Caco killed, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do remember. I was present there. That was on the 28th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can we proceed with that line of questioning where we stopped. You told us about the opposition between Caco and seemingly the police and other military authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as much as you can answer by yes, what do you know and what specifically were you present at that could tell us about the existence of this opposition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: What I know is that Caco had blocked off Bistrik as his own territory into which not even the police could go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Were you present at some opposition acts with on one side Caco's forces and on the other side, other forces, and what acts were they?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may interrupt. There is no indication with regard to the time period here as to whether these incidents "in fact" come within the indictment period or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which date was that, when was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: The animosity between Caco and the police and some other commanders of the Army of BH lasted throughout the time that I was in Sarajevo, that is until the 9th of June 1994. I know that when Caco's deputy was arrested, Pecar, I know that Caco disarmed a police station in Stari Grad, that he rounded up from the street and from the apartments 200 hostages, and that he asked for Pecar to be released or that he would kill all the hostages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since you are speaking about hostile acts, were you present during such hostile acts or conflicts? And I am not necessarily speaking about hostage situations, but conflictual situations between these two opposing sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't hostage at the time, but my neighbour, Rada, was a hostage, and she told me about this. Personally I know that Caco had fired from his headquarters with a mortar onto the other side of Bistrik where the police is, the special unit of the police, led by the special policeman, Dragan Vikic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you present when there were other similar -- when other similar shots were fired from one side or the other, but from the forces in Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But did you see any exchanges of fire from any place originating in a barracks or a military part of Sarajevo in the direction of another military part of Sarajevo in the zone under the control of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Apart from what I have mentioned, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, since we have talking about heavy weapons, I would now like to talk about destruction. My first question is as follows: In the area that you lived in, were there any mosques and were there any minarets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there several of them or just one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: In the old part of Sarajevo, including the centre, there are over 40 mosques, perhaps even more. Not a single mosque or any minarets were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, what can you tell us about the damage inflicted on buildings in Sarajevo during the period that you were there and in the areas that you were able to visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
utterances.text: The old part of town and Bistrik were parts of the town that were subjected to the greatest part of the military activity. But I can tell you that not a single building was destroyed. The only damage that was visible was damage to the roofs of houses and damage done to windows that had been shattered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, a minute ago you said that you were rounded up to dig trenches in a sense. Could you tell this Trial Chamber in relation to the damage done to property and to buildings, was the situation different at the demarcation line where you dug trenches, and in the interior where you resided or where perhaps you visited friends, et cetera? Was the situation different with regard to the damage or destruction of buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2
